lead: A steel tie rod stretches and gets thinner under load. Young's modulus E and Poisson's ratio ν capture both effects; shear modulus G and bulk modulus K describe resistance to twisting and squeezing. For an isotropic elastic material only two of the four are independent, so one tension test fixes the set. Designers use these relations for shafts, pressure vessels and springs.
prereq: You need: normal and shear stresses and Hooke's law from earlier in this unit.

sections.h3: Longitudinal strain, lateral strain and Poisson's ratio

blocks.text: A bar has original length L and lateral dimension d, say its diameter. Under axial load, length grows by ΔL and diameter shrinks by Δd. Both changes are small.

blocks.where: ε is longitudinal strain (no unit); ΔL is change in length (mm); L is original length (mm).
ε_lat is lateral strain (no unit); Δd is decrease in lateral dimension (mm); d is original lateral dimension (mm). The minus sign appears because the diameter shrinks while the length grows.

blocks.text: Poisson's ratio links them: lateral strain divided by longitudinal strain, with a minus sign so tension gives positive ν.

blocks.where: ν is Poisson's ratio (no unit); ε_lat is lateral strain; ε is longitudinal strain.

blocks.text: ν is a ratio of strains: no unit, no dimension. It belongs to the material, not the bar size.

items: Steel: ν is about 0.28 to 0.30. Aluminium: about 0.33. Copper: about 0.34.
Cork: close to 0, so when a cork is pushed into a bottle neck it is compressed radially but does not swell along its length, and it seats without jamming.
For ordinary engineering materials 0 ≤ ν ≤ 0.5. A negative ν is possible only in special auxetic materials, and ν above 0.5 is not possible for an isotropic linear elastic solid.

blocks.text: The bar also changes volume; see volumetric strain.
Here a constant means a material property independent of test-piece size. Four constants describe a linear elastic material.

blocks.where: E is Young's modulus (Pa or GPa); σ is normal stress (Pa); ε is longitudinal strain in the same direction in a uniaxial tension test. E is the slope of the straight stress-strain part.
G is shear modulus or modulus of rigidity (Pa); τ is shear stress (Pa); γ is shear strain (rad), the change in a right angle.
K is bulk modulus (Pa); p is hydrostatic pressure on all faces (Pa); ΔV/V is volumetric strain (no unit). Some syllabi call K the modulus of volumetric elasticity.

blocks.text: Isotropic means same in every direction; homogeneous means same at every point. Rolled steel sheet is nearly isotropic; wood is not, since it is much stiffer along the grain. For isotropic, homogeneous, linear elastic materials only two constants are independent. Measure any two, usually E and ν, and the rest follow.
Learn these links in both directions; exam questions give different pairs.

blocks.where: E is Young's modulus; G is shear modulus; ν is Poisson's ratio. E and G must be in the same unit; ν has no unit.
E is Young's modulus; K is bulk modulus; ν is Poisson's ratio.
E is Young's modulus; K is bulk modulus; G is shear modulus. Use this when G and K are known, for example from a torsion test and a pressure test.

blocks.text: Rearranged, the same relations give G = E / [2(1 + ν)] and K = E / [3(1 − 2ν)].

Origin: axial stress σ gives strain σ/E along the axis and −νσ/E across it. On a plane at 45°, the same stress appears as shear, with shear strain set by G. Matching the two descriptions gives E = 2G(1 + ν). Three equal compressive stresses give the K relation.
Check limits. ν = 0 gives G = E/2 and K = E/3. As ν → 0.5, 1 − 2ν → 0, so K → ∞ and the material becomes incompressible. Rubber is close: it squashes but hardly changes volume.

figure.caption: E at centre. Solid lines give E from G or K once ν is known; dashed line defines ν. Only two of the four are independent.

spec.aria: Node E at the centre, linked to G, K and the Poisson's ratio node by the standard elastic-constant relations.

examples.question: A steel alloy has E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.30. Find G and K. Verify by substituting back into E = 9KG/(3K + G).
examples.answer: G = 76.9 GPa and K = 166.7 GPa; back-substitution returns E = 200 GPa.
examples.check:
E = 200.0
nu = 0.30
G = E / (2 * (1 + nu))
K = E / (3 * (1 - 2 * nu))
print(round(G, 1))
print(round(K, 1))

code.code:
E = 200.0
nu = 0.30
G = E / (2 * (1 + nu))
K = E / (3 * (1 - 2 * nu))
print("G =", round(G, 1), "GPa")
print("K =", round(K, 1), "GPa")
print("check E =", round(9 * K * G / (3 * K + G), 1), "GPa")

examples.output:
G = 76.9 GPa
K = 166.7 GPa
check E = 200.0 GPa

traps: The minus sign in ν = −ε_lat/ε is part of the definition. In tension ε_lat is negative, so ν is positive. Dropping it gives ν = −0.30 for steel and a wrong G.

The bulk modulus relation uses 1 − 2ν, not 1 + 2ν. With ν = 0.30 the wrong sign gives 200/(3 × 1.60) = 41.7 GPa instead of 166.7 GPa. Separately, if the correct form K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)] returns a negative K, your ν is above 0.5 and is an error.
All moduli must be in the same unit before you substitute. 200 GPa and 200 000 MPa are the same stiffness; 200 and 200 000 are not. Convert first, then divide.
ν has no unit. Writing ν = 0.30 GPa loses a mark. E, G and K carry Pa.
ν cannot exceed 0.5 for an isotropic elastic solid. If working gives 0.6, look for an arithmetic slip.

quiz.q: Define Poisson's ratio and give its unit.
quiz.a: ν = −ε_lat/ε: lateral strain divided by longitudinal strain, with a minus sign so tension gives positive ν. No unit.

quiz.q: Write E in terms of G and ν.

quiz.a: It is one strain divided by another. Strain is ΔL/L, so units cancel.

quiz.q: What does ν = 0.5 mean, and what happens to K?
quiz.a: The material is incompressible: shape changes without volume change. In K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)], 1 − 2ν = 0, so K → ∞. Rubber near 0.49 is close.

quiz.q: E = 120 GPa, ν = 0.25. Find G and K.
G = 40 GPa, ν = 0.30. Find E and K.
Two steels have same E, ν = 0.28 and 0.30. Which has larger G? Larger K?
quiz.a: G = E/[2(1 + ν)]: ν = 0.28 gives larger G. K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)]: ν = 0.30 gives larger K.

quiz.q: A component has K far larger than E. What does this say about ν and the material?
quiz.a: K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)], so K ≫ E needs ν close to 0.5. The material is nearly incompressible, like rubber. Do not use ν above 0.5.

beyond: Not for exam. Finite element software stores E and ν for isotropic materials and rebuilds G and K at every element, so one wrong ν distorts the whole stiffness matrix. Auxetic materials have negative ν and are used as polymer foams and lattice metamaterials for energy absorption and implants. Rubber's ν near 0.5 needs nearly incompressible element formulations, because plain displacement elements lock. Search 'auxetic metamaterials', 'nearly incompressible hyperelasticity', 'isotropic elasticity stiffness matrix'.
